case_info.scenario: A 75-year-old man with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) with isolated deletion 5q (del5q) presented with multiple nonhealing skin ulcers on the chest and upper extremities. Four years earlier, he started taking lenalidomide, 10 mg/d (28-day cycle), to treat worsening anemia; after 2 cycles of treatment, he became transfusion independent. Since then, he has remained stable with the same dose and schedule of lenalidomide without significant adverse effects. The presenting skin lesions developed 1 month before presentation and began as small pustules that rapidly transformed into painful ulcers. He was treated with valacyclovir for a presumed diagnosis of shingles, but the lesions did not improve. Because of suspected necrotizing fasciitis, he underwent incision and drainage of the lesions. Cultures from the surgical specimen grew methicillin-resistantStaphylococcus hemolyticus. However, the lesions continued to worsen despite vancomycin and additional debridement. Thus, he was transferred to our facility. Physical examination showed multiple cutaneous ulcers with gray undermined borders and red papules of varying depths involving the chest, back, and upper extremity; lesions were as large as 9 × 15 cm. A complete blood cell count showed a white blood cell count of 16.2 × 103/μL (to convert to 109/L, multiply by 1.0) with an absolute neutrophil count of 12.7 × 103/μL, hemoglobin level of 9.4 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10.0), and platelet count of 262 × 103/μL with no circulating blasts. Results of additional laboratory studies, including blood culture and tests for herpes zoster virus (via polymerase chain reaction), antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody were all negative. Additionally, the patient also had hypertension and hypercholesterolemia for which he was taking lisinopril and simvastatin, respectively. Pathologic sampling from skin lesions demonstrated a dense dermal infiltrate with predominantly neutrophils along with reactive histiocytes, fibroblasts, and angioplasia (Figure, A). Immunohistochemical staining showed myeloperoxidase-positive neutrophils (Figure, B), histiocytic markers (CD43, CD63, CD168), and CD117-positive mast cells, but no immature myeloid precursors. Results of Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver staining were unremarkable.
case_info.caption: A, Hematoxylin-eosin staining shows polymorphonuclear neutrophils admixed with scattered histiocytes and vasculatures with a prominent endothelial lining. B, Immunohistochemical staining shows myeloperoxidase-positive neutrophils peripherally and in aggregates.
case_info.explanation: Pyoderma gangrenosum (PG) is a rare neutrophilic dermatosis (ND) characterized by painful erythematous or inflammatory papules that often progress to ulcers with a violaceous border.1A large cohort study showed that PG is commonly associated with other systemic disorders, such as inflammatory bowel disease (41% of participants), inflammatory arthropathies (21%), hematological malignancies (11%), and solid tumors (7%),2with an overall incidence of 0.63 per 100 000 person-years.3It frequently occurs in young or middle-aged adults (median age, 51.6 years) and it is more common in women.2 Cutaneous lesions in PG mimic lesions of other skin disorders, and no finding is pathognomonic for PG. Therefore, diagnosis of PG depends largely on clinical history, histological findings, and exclusion of other inflammatory or ulcerative cutaneous diseases.1,2While early-stage PG shows intradermal neutrophils and perifollicular inflammation, ulcerative PG at later stages typically demonstrates epidermal or dermal necrosis, infiltration of inflammatory cells, and abscess formation.1Deposition of IgM, C3, and fibrin can be observed in PG, but these findings are nonspecific.4There are 4 morphologic subtypes of PG. Ulcerative PG is characterized by rapid progression of inflammatory papules, pustules, or vesicles to ulcerative lesions. Bullous PG is characterized by rapid development of inflammatory bullae. Pustular PG commonly occurs in patients with inflammatory bowel disease during an acute exacerbation. Vegetative PG is characterized by localized and superficial lesions with an indolent disease course.1 The pathogenesis of PG depends primarily on immune dysregulation and genetic factors. Previous studies have shown that gene expression levels of proinflammatory cytokines (eg, tumor necrosis factor α and interleukins [ILs] IL-1α, IL-1β, IL-8, IL-12, IL-15, IL-17, IL-23, and IL-36) and levels of pattern recognition receptors are increased in the cutaneous lesions of PG, leading to activation of inflammasomes and dysregulation of innate and adaptive immunities.1Furthermore, several reports from familial cases of PG suggest that genetic factors can play important roles in PG pathogenesis,5and variants inPTSTPIP1/CD2BP1, MEFV, NLRP3, NLRP12, NOD2,andLPIN2have been reported in PG.1 Among hematological cancers associated with PG, 10% to 20% of patients with MDS develop autoimmune manifestations that include NDs, systemic lupus erythematosus, Behçet disease, and vasculitis.6Chromosomal abnormalities commonly identified in patients with MDS and their autoimmune manifestations include del5q (22.6% of participants in one study),7in which haploinsufficiency ofRPS14from del5q upregulates S100A9, a DAMP (damage-associated molecular pattern) protein, that plays essential roles in chronic inflammation and innate immunity.8Notably, ND was associated with significantly adverse survival outcomes in patients with MDS in multivariate analyses (hazard ratio, 1.79; 95% CI, 1.03-3.09;P= .04),7although other studies found that overall prognosis was more closely related to the IPSS (International Prognostic Scoring System) category than to the underlying autoimmune process.9In addition, PG has been reported to be associated with lenalidomide, an immunomodulatory drug that is commonly used to treat MDS, multiple myeloma, and lymphomas,10although the exact frequency of PG associated with lenalidomide remains to be determined. Treatment of PG varies depending on severity and extent of involved cutaneous lesions. First-line treatment for limited disease includes topical corticosteroid or tacrolimus.1For patients with extensive or rapidly progressing disease, a systemic steroid (0.5-1.5 mg/kg/d of prednisone or its equivalent, then taper over 4-6 weeks) or cyclosporin (in patients who cannot tolerate systemic steroids) is recommended as the first-line treatment, and adjunctive agents (eg, infliximab, azathioprine, mycophenolate) can be added to prevent disease flare during steroid taper.1In cases of refractory disease, intravenous immunoglobulin or alkylating agents (eg, cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil) could be an option, although many other agents (eg, melphalan, thalidomide, canakinumab, tocilizumab) have been reported to be effective.1 In this patient, lenalidomide was discontinued and he was treated with methylprednisolone, 1 mg/kg/d, and infliximab, 5 mg/kg. Skin lesions improved considerably and there has been no recurrence.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):

  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",

  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

Four years earlier, he started taking lenalidomide, 10 mg/d (28-day cycle), to treat worsening anemia; after 2 cycles of treatment, he became transfusion independent. Since then, he has remained stable with the same dose and schedule of lenalidomide without significant adverse effects. The presenting skin lesions developed 1 month before presentation and began as small pustules that rapidly transformed into painful ulcers. He was treated with valacyclovir for a presumed diagnosis of shingles, but the lesions did not improve. Because of suspected necrotizing fasciitis, he underwent incision and drainage of the lesions. Cultures from the surgical specimen grew methicillin-resistantStaphylococcus hemolyticus. However, the lesions continued to worsen despite vancomycin and additional debridement. Thus, he was transferred to our facility. Physical examination showed multiple cutaneous ulcers with gray undermined borders and red papules of varying depths involving the chest, back, and upper extremity; lesions were as large as 9 × 15 cm. A complete blood cell count showed a white blood cell count of 16.2 × 103/μL (to convert to 109/L, multiply by 1.0) with an absolute neutrophil count of 12.7 × 103/μL, hemoglobin level of 9.4 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10.0), and platelet count of 262 × 103/μL with no circulating blasts. Results of additional laboratory studies, including blood culture and tests for herpes zoster virus (via polymerase chain reaction), antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody were all negative. Additionally, the patient also had hypertension and hypercholesterolemia for which he was taking lisinopril and simvastatin, respectively. Pathologic sampling from skin lesions demonstrated a dense dermal infiltrate with predominantly neutrophils along with reactive histiocytes, fibroblasts, and angioplasia (Figure, A). Immunohistochemical staining showed myeloperoxidase-positive neutrophils (Figure, B), histiocytic markers (CD43, CD63, CD168), and CD117-positive mast cells, but no immature myeloid precursors. Results of Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver staining were unremarkable.

case_info.explanation: Pyoderma gangrenosum (PG) is a rare neutrophilic dermatosis (ND) characterized by painful erythematous or inflammatory papules that often progress to ulcers with a violaceous border.1A large cohort study showed that PG is commonly associated with other systemic disorders, such as inflammatory bowel disease (41% of participants), inflammatory arthropathies (21%), hematological malignancies (11%), and solid tumors (7%),2with an overall incidence of 0.63 per 100 000 person-years.3It frequently occurs in young or middle-aged adults (median age, 51.6 years) and it is more common in women.2 Cutaneous lesions in PG mimic lesions of other skin disorders, and no finding is pathognomonic for PG. Therefore, diagnosis of PG depends largely on clinical history, histological findings, and exclusion of other inflammatory or ulcerative cutaneous diseases.1,2While early-stage PG shows intradermal neutrophils and perifollicular inflammation, ulcerative PG at later stages typically demonstrates epidermal or dermal necrosis, infiltration of inflammatory cells, and abscess formation.1Deposition of IgM, C3, and fibrin can be observed in PG, but these findings are nonspecific.4There are 4 morphologic subtypes of PG. Ulcerative PG is characterized by rapid progression of inflammatory papules, pustules, or vesicles to ulcerative lesions. Bullous PG is characterized by rapid development of inflammatory bullae. Pustular PG commonly occurs in patients with inflammatory bowel disease during an acute exacerbation. Vegetative PG is characterized by localized and superficial lesions with an indolent disease course.1 The pathogenesis of PG depends primarily on immune dysregulation and genetic factors. Previous studies have shown that gene expression levels of proinflammatory cytokines (eg, tumor necrosis factor α and interleukins [ILs] IL-1α, IL-1β, IL-8, IL-12, IL-15, IL-17, IL-23, and IL-36) and levels of pattern recognition receptors are increased in the cutaneous lesions of PG, leading to activation of inflammasomes and dysregulation of innate and adaptive immunities.1Furthermore, several reports from familial cases of PG suggest that genetic factors can play important roles in PG pathogenesis,5and variants inPTSTPIP1/CD2BP1, MEFV, NLRP3, NLRP12, NOD2,andLPIN2have been reported in PG.1 Among hematological cancers associated with PG, 10% to 20% of patients with MDS develop autoimmune manifestations that include NDs, systemic lupus erythematosus, Behçet disease, and vasculitis.6Chromosomal abnormalities commonly identified in patients with MDS and their autoimmune manifestations include del5q (22.6% of participants in one study),7in which haploinsufficiency ofRPS14from del5q upregulates S100A9, a DAMP (damage-associated molecular pattern) protein, that plays essential roles in chronic inflammation and innate immunity.8Notably, ND was associated with significantly adverse survival outcomes in patients with MDS in multivariate analyses (hazard ratio, 1.79; 95% CI, 1.03-3.09;P= .04),7although other studies found that overall prognosis was more closely related to the IPSS (International Prognostic Scoring System) category than to the underlying autoimmune process.9In addition, PG has been reported to be associated with lenalidomide, an immunomodulatory drug that is commonly used to treat MDS, multiple myeloma, and lymphomas,10although the exact frequency of PG associated with lenalidomide remains to be determined. Treatment of PG varies depending on severity and extent of involved cutaneous lesions. First-line treatment for limited disease includes topical corticosteroid or tacrolimus.1For patients with extensive or rapidly progressing disease, a systemic steroid (0.5-1.5 mg/kg/d of prednisone or its equivalent, then taper over 4-6 weeks) or cyclosporin (in patients who cannot tolerate systemic steroids) is recommended as the first-line treatment, and adjunctive agents (eg, infliximab, azathioprine, mycophenolate) can be added to prevent disease flare during steroid taper.1In cases of refractory disease, intravenous immunoglobulin or alkylating agents (eg, cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil) could be an option, although many other agents (eg, melphalan, thalidomide, canakinumab, tocilizumab) have been reported to be effective.1 In this patient, lenalidomide was discontinued and he was treated with methylprednisolone, 1 mg/kg/d, and infliximab, 5 mg/kg. Skin lesions improved considerably and there has been no recurrence.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

A 75-year-old man with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) with isolated deletion 5q (del5q) presented with multiple nonhealing skin ulcers on the chest and upper extremities. Four years earlier, he started taking lenalidomide, 10 mg/d (28-day cycle), to treat worsening anemia; after 2 cycles of treatment, he became transfusion independent. Since then, he has remained stable with the same dose and schedule of lenalidomide without significant adverse effects. The presenting skin lesions developed 1 month before presentation and began as small pustules that rapidly transformed into painful ulcers. He was treated with valacyclovir for a presumed diagnosis of shingles, but the lesions did not improve. Because of suspected necrotizing fasciitis, he underwent incision and drainage of the lesions. Cultures from the surgical specimen grew methicillin-resistantStaphylococcus hemolyticus. However, the lesions continued to worsen despite vancomycin and additional debridement. Thus, he was transferred to our facility. Physical examination showed multiple cutaneous ulcers with gray undermined borders and red papules of varying depths involving the chest, back, and upper extremity; lesions were as large as 9 × 15 cm. A complete blood cell count showed a white blood cell count of 16.2 × 103/μL (to convert to 109/L, multiply by 1.0) with an absolute neutrophil count of 12.7 × 103/μL, hemoglobin level of 9.4 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10.0), and platelet count of 262 × 103/μL with no circulating blasts. Results of additional laboratory studies, including blood culture and tests for herpes zoster virus (via polymerase chain reaction), antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody were all negative. Additionally, the patient also had hypertension and hypercholesterolemia for which he was taking lisinopril and simvastatin, respectively. Pathologic sampling from skin lesions demonstrated a dense dermal infiltrate with predominantly neutrophils along with reactive histiocytes, fibroblasts, and angioplasia (Figure, A). Immunohistochemical staining showed myeloperoxidase-positive neutrophils (Figure, B), histiocytic markers (CD43, CD63, CD168), and CD117-positive mast cells, but no immature myeloid precursors. Results of Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver staining were unremarkable.

case_info.explanation: Pyoderma gangrenosum (PG) is a rare neutrophilic dermatosis (ND) characterized by painful erythematous or inflammatory papules that often progress to ulcers with a violaceous border.1A large cohort study showed that PG is commonly associated with other systemic disorders, such as inflammatory bowel disease (41% of participants), inflammatory arthropathies (21%), hematological malignancies (11%), and solid tumors (7%),2with an overall incidence of 0.63 per 100 000 person-years.3It frequently occurs in young or middle-aged adults (median age, 51.6 years) and it is more common in women.2 Cutaneous lesions in PG mimic lesions of other skin disorders, and no finding is pathognomonic for PG. Therefore, diagnosis of PG depends largely on clinical history, histological findings, and exclusion of other inflammatory or ulcerative cutaneous diseases.1,2While early-stage PG shows intradermal neutrophils and perifollicular inflammation, ulcerative PG at later stages typically demonstrates epidermal or dermal necrosis, infiltration of inflammatory cells, and abscess formation.1Deposition of IgM, C3, and fibrin can be observed in PG, but these findings are nonspecific.4There are 4 morphologic subtypes of PG. Ulcerative PG is characterized by rapid progression of inflammatory papules, pustules, or vesicles to ulcerative lesions. Bullous PG is characterized by rapid development of inflammatory bullae. Pustular PG commonly occurs in patients with inflammatory bowel disease during an acute exacerbation. Vegetative PG is characterized by localized and superficial lesions with an indolent disease course.1 The pathogenesis of PG depends primarily on immune dysregulation and genetic factors. Previous studies have shown that gene expression levels of proinflammatory cytokines (eg, tumor necrosis factor α and interleukins [ILs] IL-1α, IL-1β, IL-8, IL-12, IL-15, IL-17, IL-23, and IL-36) and levels of pattern recognition receptors are increased in the cutaneous lesions of PG, leading to activation of inflammasomes and dysregulation of innate and adaptive immunities.1Furthermore, several reports from familial cases of PG suggest that genetic factors can play important roles in PG pathogenesis,5and variants inPTSTPIP1/CD2BP1, MEFV, NLRP3, NLRP12, NOD2,andLPIN2have been reported in PG.1 Among hematological cancers associated with PG, 10% to 20% of patients with MDS develop autoimmune manifestations that include NDs, systemic lupus erythematosus, Behçet disease, and vasculitis.6Chromosomal abnormalities commonly identified in patients with MDS and their autoimmune manifestations include del5q (22.6% of participants in one study),7in which haploinsufficiency ofRPS14from del5q upregulates S100A9, a DAMP (damage-associated molecular pattern) protein, that plays essential roles in chronic inflammation and innate immunity.8Notably, ND was associated with significantly adverse survival outcomes in patients with MDS in multivariate analyses (hazard ratio, 1.79; 95% CI, 1.03-3.09;P= .04),7although other studies found that overall prognosis was more closely related to the IPSS (International Prognostic Scoring System) category than to the underlying autoimmune process.9In addition, PG has been reported to be associated with lenalidomide, an immunomodulatory drug that is commonly used to treat MDS, multiple myeloma, and lymphomas,10although the exact frequency of PG associated with lenalidomide remains to be determined. Treatment of PG varies depending on severity and extent of involved cutaneous lesions. First-line treatment for limited disease includes topical corticosteroid or tacrolimus.1For patients with extensive or rapidly progressing disease, a systemic steroid (0.5-1.5 mg/kg/d of prednisone or its equivalent, then taper over 4-6 weeks) or cyclosporin (in patients who cannot tolerate systemic steroids) is recommended as the first-line treatment, and adjunctive agents (eg, infliximab, azathioprine, mycophenolate) can be added to prevent disease flare during steroid taper.1In cases of refractory disease, intravenous immunoglobulin or alkylating agents (eg, cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil) could be an option, although many other agents (eg, melphalan, thalidomide, canakinumab, tocilizumab) have been reported to be effective.1 In this patient, lenalidomide was discontinued and he was treated with methylprednisolone, 1 mg/kg/d, and infliximab, 5 mg/kg. You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

Since then, he has remained stable with the same dose and schedule of lenalidomide without significant adverse effects. The presenting skin lesions developed 1 month before presentation and began as small pustules that rapidly transformed into painful ulcers. He was treated with valacyclovir for a presumed diagnosis of shingles, but the lesions did not improve. Because of suspected necrotizing fasciitis, he underwent incision and drainage of the lesions. Cultures from the surgical specimen grew methicillin-resistantStaphylococcus hemolyticus. However, the lesions continued to worsen despite vancomycin and additional debridement. Physical examination showed multiple cutaneous ulcers with gray undermined borders and red papules of varying depths involving the chest, back, and upper extremity; lesions were as large as 9 × 15 cm. Additionally, the patient also had hypertension and hypercholesterolemia for which he was taking lisinopril and simvastatin, respectively. Immunohistochemical staining showed myeloperoxidase-positive neutrophils (Figure, B), histiocytic markers (CD43, CD63, CD168), and CD117-positive mast cells, but no immature myeloid precursors. Results of Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver staining were unremarkable.
